source: Jannach & Schmitz (2016; ASE journal) Model-based diagnosis of spreadsheet programs: user study
finding: Spreadsheet turned into a constraint problem. Reiter hitting-set search finds formulas that could explain a wrong output. Lab study: tool users found the planted error far more often and faster.
numbers: N=24 CS students, between subjects, one spreadsheet with 16 formula cells, one error (duplicate cell reference in O9), 15 min cap. With tool: 100% success, 163 s total (SD 78; 66 s start-up, 97 s find). Without tool (plain Excel): 67% success, 547 s mean (SD 269) among solvers. Difference significant p<0.05.
limits: Authors call it preliminary: students, one small sheet, one error, one injected error type. Fastest no-tool person took 2.5 min, below the tool group mean.
agent_relevance: Shows that a code-computed list of suspects beats unaided search even for people who understand the artefact. Supports S5 locating the fault by code, not by opinion.

source: Jannach & Schmitz (2016) performance experiments
finding: Speed-ups for diagnosis: parallel threads and input-dependency pruning cut run time a lot. Realistic sheets with several hundred formulas diagnosed in under a second; deep multi-fault cases cost seconds.
numbers: Parallelisation gained 0% for tiny problems up to 30% for the hardest (50 products, 150 constraints, double fault). Dependency analysis gained 50-60%. Overall more than 70%: 2.2 s down to about 630 ms. Sales forecast sheet (over 140 formulas): under 0.5 s. 700+ formula sheet, 3 faults, depth limit 3: under 4 s.
limits: Search depth is capped at 3 because diagnoses with 4+ faulty formulas are judged too hard for users to understand. Mutation-injected errors, not natural ones. Cost grows fast with number of simultaneous faults.
agent_relevance: A cap on fault cardinality (single fault first, then double) is a practical rule for our S5: do not enumerate huge multi-fault sets.

source: Schmitz, Hofer, Jannach, Wotawa (2016) Fragment-based diagnosis of spreadsheets
finding: Grouping cells into fragments (copy-equivalent formulas merged) shrinks the candidate list and run time. Extra test cases on the few suspect fragments then pinpoint the true cell every time.
numbers: 5 spreadsheets. Course planning: cell-based diagnosis took 11,903 ms with 2,304 diagnoses; fragment level took about 14 ms and returned 2 fragment diagnoses; then additional fragment test cases located the cause exactly (1 diagnosis) in all 5 sheets. About half of fragments were reported as possible causes.
limits: Only 5 sheets, simulated user who gives perfect values for interim cells. Authors say a larger evaluation is future work. Real users may give wrong test values.
agent_relevance: Hierarchical diagnosis (coarse unit first, then refine inside suspects) is a cheap way to reduce the suspect set before asking the model to look. Fits S5 then S7.

source: Schmitz & Jannach (2017) An AI-based interactive tool for spreadsheet debugging (EXQUISITE)
finding: Tool paper summarising their studies: partial test cases on fragments make debugging more efficient. The add-in lets users answer targeted questions chosen to separate suspects with few interactions.
numbers: No new numbers. States that the between-subjects study showed faster location with the tool and that some non-tool users never found the fault. Tool still a research prototype, not in commercial Excel.
limits: Self-report of its own studies. No effect sizes given. No field evidence of adoption.
agent_relevance: Sequential question asking (pick the next test that best splits suspects) is the human-facing form of our S7.

source: Jannach, Baharloo, Williamson (2013) Toward an integrated framework for declarative and interactive spreadsheet debugging
finding: Early version of the constraint-based approach. Related-work text says rival GoalDebug was judged by the share of correct repairs and the rank of the right repair, on mutated real sheets.
numbers: Skimmed; no headline numbers recorded beyond the design and related work.
limits: Mutation-based evaluation. Skimmed only. Weak evidence on its own.
agent_relevance: Mutation testing is the standard way to get ground truth for diagnosis; same idea can score our S5 on planted bugs.

source: Rodler (2016) Interactive Debugging of Knowledge Bases (dissertation): query selection
finding: Knowledge-base debugging asks a domain expert yes/no questions about what should hold. Choosing the question matters hugely. Entropy-based choice with a rough fault guess beats split-in-half, and both beat random. A learning strategy (RIO) protects against bad fault guesses.
numbers: Bad fault information plus a poor query strategy can cost over 2000% more user effort than a good strategy. RIO was at least as good as the best other strategy in 100% of the hardest test KBs and better than all others in more than 70% of them. Best case: factor up to 23, i.e. over 95% of user effort saved.
limits: Evaluated on benchmark and real ontologies with simulated users who answer correctly; the user's own errors are not modelled. Quality of the fault guess is only known after the session ends.
agent_relevance: Strong support for choosing the next test by information gain, and for a fallback when the prior over faults is unreliable. Directly relevant to S7.

source: Rodler (2016) dissertation: human difficulty with inconsistency
finding: Cites a study where people tried to decide whether an entailment holds in a 3-formula description-logic knowledge base. Even experts with many years of experience, including reasoner developers, did not see it.
numbers: Three formulas only. Participants included DL reasoner developers. Participant count not given in the passage read.
limits: Reported second-hand from an earlier study. Not re-read in the original.
agent_relevance: Even experts cannot find the cause of a fault by inspection. This is why code-computed conflicts should replace model opinion at S5.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A quantitative and qualitative evaluation of LLM-based explainable fault localization (AutoFL)
finding: LLM that navigates a repository with function calls beats classic spectrum-based fault localisation at acc@1 (top guess right), but loses at acc@3 and acc@5 with GPT-3.5. GPT-4 fixes that.
numbers: 798 real bugs, Defects4J (353) and BugsInPy. Method-level acc@1 up 19.7% over Ochiai on Defects4J and 166.7% on BugsInPy with GPT-3.5; 233.3% with GPT-4 on BugsInPy. One GPT-4 run beat five merged GPT-3.5 runs. About 16 s per bug (GPT-3.5, Defects4J).
limits: Authors argue memorisation is not the sole cause but do not rule leakage out. GPT-3.5 loses at acc@3 and acc@5. Needs a test and the repo, not just the code.
agent_relevance: A tool-using loop with function calls to get real code is better than prompting alone. Supports G2: revise from real output.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) AutoFL: consistency as confidence
finding: Repeating the LLM run and measuring agreement gives a confidence signal that filters out false positives. More runs raise accuracy a lot.
numbers: Confidence score = share of runs agreeing on the top prediction. Merging more runs improved accuracy on both benchmarks; fewer than 10% of runs used the maximum of 10 calls.
limits: Agreement among samples of one model is not independent evidence (our G4); it is a hint, not proof. Authors only use it to rank and filter.
agent_relevance: Usable as a cheap confidence flag, never as proof. Matches G4.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) AutoFL: explanation quality
finding: LLM explanations of the bug are often wrong or empty. Only a fifth are accurate. Developers liked a few good explanations, disliked many, and were misled by wrong fix suggestions.
numbers: 300 explanations from 60 bugs: 20% accurate, 26.3% contain at least one inaccurate statement, 46.7% bland (restate test and covered methods). Per bug, 56.7% had at least one accurate explanation. 83.7% of runs produced any explanation (others hit token or call limits). Developer interviews, small group.
limits: Manual grading by the authors (agreement 86.5% before discussion). Small interview sample. Java and Python only.
agent_relevance: A located fault with a wrong story is a hazard. Require the story to cite failing output (G2) and score it by code.

source: Wu, Li, Zhang, Papadakis, Harman, Liu (2023) Large language models in fault localisation
finding: ChatGPT-4 at function level beats the best prior method when given the error log. When code context grows to class level, it falls well behind. Error log is the single most useful input.
numbers: Defects4J, 6 Java projects, 5 repeats. Function-level with error log: average 46.9% higher acc@1 than SmartFL. Class-level: 49.9% lower acc@1 than SmartFL. Dropping the error log cut ChatGPT-4 acc@1 by 25.6%. New leak-free set StuDefects: 52.9% better than the baseline.
limits: ChatGPT versions of 2023; Java only; ChatGPT-3.5 comparable to baselines. Run-to-run variance is present (ChatGPT-4 with log acc@1 ranged roughly 135 to 145 across repeats).
agent_relevance: Two lessons: real failing output matters most (G2), and long context kills localisation. Narrow the suspect scope before asking (S5 after a code filter).

source: Wu et al. (2023) test for training-data leakage (StuDefects)
finding: To check that Defects4J was not memorised, the authors built a new set of student bugs from after the model's data cut-off. ChatGPT still beat the baseline there.
numbers: StuDefects result: 52.9% superiority over the state of the art on acc@1. Also ChatGPT is worse than baseline at class level on Defects4J, which would not happen if it simply memorised answers.
limits: Student programs differ from Defects4J in style and size. Authors' own argument for no leakage, not a formal proof.
agent_relevance: Good practice for us: test on items created after the model's cut-off or mutated, so a pass is on something not fitted (G3).

source: AgentFL (2024) Scaling LLM-based fault localization to project-level context
finding: Multi-agent LLM pipeline with test-behaviour tracking, document-guided search and multi-round dialogue localises 157 of 395 Defects4J bugs at top-1. It is complementary to learned methods but gains little at top-3 and top-5.
numbers: Defects4J v1.2.0, 395 bugs: Top-1 157, Top-3 183, Top-5 187. ChatGPT-with-Ochiai baseline 121 at top-1; LLMAO with Ochiai 129 at top-1. Abstract: 28 more than the next LLM-based method at top-1.
limits: Result lists are short (often fewer than 3 suspects), so top-3 and top-5 gains are small. One benchmark. Leakage not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Staged analysis helps. A ranked list from code is complementary to an LLM guess; merge, do not replace.

source: Xia, Deng, Dunn, Zhang (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: A fixed three-step pipeline (localise, repair, validate), with no agent choosing actions, matched or beat open-source autonomous agents on SWE-bench Lite at low cost. The program decides the flow, the model fills slots.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite 300 issues: 96 fixed (32.00%), average cost $0.70. Manual audit of the benchmark found 4.3% of issues with the exact patch in the text, 10.0% with missing key information, 5.0% with misleading solutions. Cleaned set SWE-bench Lite-S has 249 problems.
limits: Gains are on one benchmark and later models surpassed it. Benchmark noise (around 19% problematic items) limits all comparisons.
agent_relevance: Strong match for our design principle: the program decides every transition, the model fills a slot (section 1 of SCHEMA). Also warns to audit benchmarks.

source: Huang et al. (2024; ICLR) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Reported self-correction gains came from using the ground-truth label to decide when to stop. Without that label, asking the model to review its own answer made accuracy go down.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7 after two rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5.
limits: Reasoning tasks (math, QA), not code with test output. Authors say self-correction can work with external feedback. Prompts of 2023.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and G1: revise only from real external output, not from the model's own doubt.

source: Olausson, Inala, Wang, Gao, Solar-Lezama (2024; ICLR) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Self-repair of code gives small, uneven gains once its cost is counted; the bottleneck is the quality of the model's feedback about why the code failed. Better feedback from a stronger model or a human helps a lot.
numbers: HumanEval and APPS, Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. GPT-4 repair success with human feedback 52.60% vs 33.30% with GPT-4's own feedback (introductory 62.21 vs 42.64; interview 45.67 vs 19.33; competition 14.67 vs 3.67). Stronger-model feedback let weaker models beat both their baselines and their own self-repair.
limits: Small human study (expert programmers). Gains judged at equal sample cost, not at equal wall time. Unit-test style tasks only.
agent_relevance: Debug explanation is the weak link. A cheaper good diagnostician (code localisation, or a separate checker) is worth more than extra repair samples.

source: Chen, Lin, Schaerli, Zhou (2024; ICLR) Teaching large language models to self-debug
finding: With execution feedback and a short code explanation (rubber-duck style), few-shot self-debugging raises accuracy. The more concrete the execution evidence, the larger the gain.
numbers: Spider: Codex 81.3 to 84.1 with explanation (GPT-3.5 71.1 to 72.2, GPT-4 73.2 to 73.6). TransCoder (C++ to Python): Codex 80.4 baseline; with unit-test feedback 92.5; GPT-4 77.3 to 90.4. MBPP: GPT-4 72.8 to 80.6. Simple right/wrong feedback gave much less than unit-test plus trace feedback.
limits: Gains on Spider are small (2-3%) when there are no unit tests. Few-shot prompts matter; GPT-4 followed exemplars worse than Codex on Spider.
agent_relevance: Revision pays when real execution output exists; a bare pass/fail signal gives only a small lift. Supports G2.

source: Gou et al. (2024; ICLR) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
finding: Letting the model check its output with external tools (code interpreter, search) and then revise works. The same loop without the tool gives limited, unstable and sometimes negative changes.
numbers: GSM8K ChatGPT: PoT 72.5, +CRITIC 78.2 (always correct) and 83.9 (oracle trigger). text-davinci-003: CRITIC without tool -1.8 (68.3 vs 70.1). Self-Refine on Codex PAL 71.3 went to 26.7 (-44.6) in the no-tool setting. Gains grow with model size (TabMWP +4.7, +9.4, +16.0 for 7B, 13B, 70B).
limits: Task choice (math, QA, toxicity). Some comparisons use others' reported numbers.
agent_relevance: Same conclusion as Huang et al.: an external check is what makes revision pay off.

source: Ma et al. (2024; NeurIPS D&B) SpreadsheetBench: overall
finding: On 912 real spreadsheet-manipulation questions from Excel forums, models do far worse than people. The best LLM and Copilot in Excel solved only about a fifth.
numbers: Soft-restriction overall accuracy: GPT-4o 18.35% single round, 16.96% multi-round; Copilot in Excel about 20% (small sample); SheetCopilot (GPT-4) 14%; GPT-3.5 2.34 (7.09 multi-round); DeepseekCoder 33B 2.60 (5.31); Llama-3 70B 1.32 (3.74); human Excel experts 71.33% (hard restriction 62.00%). Four annotators.
limits: Task is manipulation (write a solution), not fault finding. Online-judge style tests with several files each. Copilot and SheetCopilot numbers on a smaller sample.
agent_relevance: Large gap between models and humans on real spreadsheets, even before debugging. Real data is much harder than synthetic.

source: Ma et al. (2024) SpreadsheetBench: multi-round feedback
finding: More rounds with code-execution error feedback helped weak models a lot (some nearly tenfold) but did not help the strongest model.
numbers: CodeQwen 0.51 to 3.66 overall; Llama-3 70B 1.32 to 3.74; GPT-3.5 2.34 to 7.09. GPT-4o dropped 18.35 to 16.96. GPT-3.5 improved as rounds rose from 2 to 4; GPT-4o did not. Authors explain GPT-4o's first answers were already executable.
limits: Cause of the GPT-4o drop is the authors' explanation (duplicate row retrieval). Not tested directly.
agent_relevance: The value of a revision loop depends on how bad the first try is. Do not force loops when the first answer already passes its checks (G1).

source: FLAME (2023) A small language model for spreadsheet formulas
finding: A 60-million-parameter model trained only on Excel formulas competes with models up to 175B on formula repair and completion.
numbers: T5-small based, 60M parameters. Beats other models in 10 of 14 repair and completion settings. Repair benchmark: 273 labelled Excel formulas from help forums plus 500 synthetic; scored by exact match in top-1 and top-5.
limits: Repairs are last-mile (syntax and simple semantic errors, few edits), not finding which of many cells is wrong. Exact per-setting numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: A small specialised helper for formula-level fixes could be called as a tool at S5 after code has found the cell.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which agent causes task failures and when? (Who&When): headline
finding: Asking LLMs to find which agent and which step caused a multi-agent failure works poorly, much like diagnosis by opinion. Step finding is near chance in many settings and falls to near 0 with long logs.
numbers: 127 multi-agent systems. Best method: 53.5% agent-level, 14.2% step-level. Best on hand-crafted systems: 8.77% step-level. Some methods score below random. All three methods fall to near 0% step accuracy at maximum context length.
limits: Annotators were uncertain on 15-30% of items and disagreed. Log-reading task, no executable model of the system. Prompting only.
agent_relevance: LLM-only fault attribution is unreliable. Strong case for code-computed conflicts (hitting sets) at S5 rather than asking the model who failed.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Who&When: reasoning models
finding: Stronger reasoning models did not fix failure attribution. DeepSeek R1 beat GPT-4o in only 1 of 4 metric cells and o1 did not beat it consistently.
numbers: Hand-crafted systems, Table 4. All-at-once: GPT-4o 54.31 agent / 4.39 step; o1 41.38 / 10.34; R1 56.90 / 3.45. Step-by-step: GPT-4o 33.62 / 7.90; o1 36.21 / 13.79; R1 32.76 / 6.90.
limits: Prompt for o1 had to be modified after a policy flag. Small hand-crafted subset.
agent_relevance: More thinking tokens alone does not give a diagnosis. Consistent with using code for localisation.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Who&When: method comparison
finding: No single prompting method wins. All-at-once is best for naming the agent (big context), step-by-step best for naming the step (fine grain). Binary search sits in between.
numbers: All-at-once agent-level accuracy 19.13% and 20.69% higher than step-by-step with ground truth; step-by-step best at step level. A tolerance of a few steps raised step accuracy. Accuracy falls as log context grows.
limits: Same ordering held on other LLMs on the hand-crafted subset only (cost).
agent_relevance: Mirrors the hierarchical idea in fragment-based spreadsheet diagnosis: coarse stage then fine stage. Suggests a two-stage S5.

source: Parnin & Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers? (ISSTA)
finding: Classic human-study boundary condition: automated fault localisation tools that look good in rank-based benchmarks did not clearly help programmers on harder tasks.
numbers: From memory only. Not verified this session.
limits: Not opened. Treat as a lead; check the paper before citing numbers.
agent_relevance: Benchmark rank gains may not transfer to real use. Test end to end, not only on rank.

source: Pearson et al. (2017) Evaluating and improving fault localization (ICSE)
finding: Re-evaluation of earlier fault localisation claims on real faults rather than only artificial ones. Results on artificial faults did not always carry over to real ones.
numbers: From memory only. Exact figures not verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Planted-bug scores may overstate real performance. Keep a real-failure set for S5 tests.

source: GoalDebug (Abraham & Erwig) as described in Jannach & Schmitz (2016)
finding: Competing spreadsheet debugger proposes repairs from user-given expected values, ranked by heuristic rules. Its quality depends on hand-built change-inference rules; the model-based approach is domain independent.
numbers: Evaluation (as reported): spreadsheets mutated with spreadsheet-specific operators; measured the share of correct repairs and the rank of the right repair.
limits: Second-hand description, not the original paper.
agent_relevance: A rival design: rule-based repair proposals versus model-based fault finding. We would use code-based finding first and model-based repair second.

source: Jannach & Schmitz (2016): limits of the model-based approach
finding: The approach covers faults in formulas only. It needs at least one test case with expected values, and the user must read and trust the candidate list. Higher-cardinality faults are costly and hard to read.
numbers: Search depth limited to 3 levels in tests. Single-fault and double-fault scenarios tested. 24-student study with one sheet. Authors name spectrum-based methods and Hofer et al. as complements.
limits: Authors' own limitation section. No large field study. Corpus: EUSES sheets plus some from their own institute.
agent_relevance: Diagnosis needs an oracle for expected values. Without a trusted expected output our S5 cannot run; the same limit applies to our agent.
